chunk_text: Globally, an explicit link of orogenic gold with black shale has been recognized for some time (e.g. Keppie et al . 1986; Large et al . 2011; Tomkins 2013; Parnell et al . 2017, 2018; Gaboury 2021; Gaboury et al . 2021; Chen et al . 2022; Ding et al . 2023; Goldfarb and Pitcairn 2023). Locally, the association has been recognized in the Welsh gold belt (Annels and Roberts 1989; Mason et al . 2002) and in the SUDLT at Clontibret (Fig. 2). Furthermore, gold speciation studies have recognized a ' gold only ' model (Pokrovski et al . 2014), wherein Au occurs with As but only minor amounts of other base metal sulfides. In ground adjacent to our project area, follow-up of reconnaissance drainage anomalies by soil sampling (Shaw et al . 1995) detected a close association between gold enrichment and broader zones of elevated As; in contrast, direct spatial associations between gold and the base metals and antimony were not evident. Understanding of the ' gold only ' model has been deepened by detailed studies of both contemporary processes and their geological expression (Large et al . 2011; Lin et al . 2016; Zhao et al . 2018, 2020; Wu et al . 2020; Gómez-Fernández et al . 2021). These involve the initial capture of Au and As in diagenetic framboidal pyrite by bacterial sulfate reduction and inorganic sulfate reduction in anoxic basin conditions. Subsequent release to hydrothermal fluids occurs during lithification and low-grade metamorphism. The SUDLT contains the Lower Paleozoic muddy turbidite sandstones of the Gala Group and the Moffat Shale, which are examples of black shales with relatively high carbonaceous content reflecting anoxic conditions (Parnell et al . 2023).

Reference should be made to Supplementary material, SI 5 for further detail supporting the data reported in this section. After drainage of the deepest water, thus providing direct access to all parts of the mine, it was possible to confirm the main conclusions of Shaw et al . (1995); specifically, that only millimetre-scale malachite veination (Fig. 17b) exists in level B and C and that the Cu staining in level C is probably unrelated to the reported pyrite - arsenopyrite occurrence within the ' F zone 10 - 20 cm ' ( sensu Shaw et al . 1995) in level B of the mine. No minerals of economic value exist in the mine and there is no spoil heap. This may be explained by the widespread occurrence of ' coalite ' workings across the SUDLT (Parnell et al . 2023, 2024); Hoardweel may be a local expression of the working of high total organic carbon (TOC %) pelites for ' coalite ' , as reported from other terranes (Zheng et al . 2018). Detailed study of the pyrite - arsenopyrite occurrence within the ' F zone 10 - 20 cm ' (Fig. 17) in level B provides important insights. Samples taken from the zone had yielded a maximum of 1333 ppb Au (Shaw et al . 1995) and 640 ppb Au (this study). Optical microscopy of a sample from the zone (Fig. 18a) had noted that the rock contained quartz, biotite and hornblende accompanied by patches of heavily sericitized feldspars with sub-millimetre-scale arsenopyrite veination.

The IP section of L2 reveals intermittent zones of high chargeability between stations 0-21 (0-560 meters), where the highest values potentially associated with gold mineralization are found at 50-250 meters. Two features within this line, at shallow and intermediate depths, are interpreted as quartz-adularia veins.

chunk_text: As described above, remobilization at Jacobina clearly led to a change in gold composition with Ag-depletion by postdepositional fluids. Compared with other metaconglomeratehosted gold deposits, the Jacobina gold has a unique composition characterized by the following: (a) relatively low Ag content, (b) presence of Cu in low concentrations, and (c) absence of Hg. The Witwatersrand gold has been reported in several studies to contain far higher Ag and Hg contents between 0.3-32.1wt% and 0.5-5.9 wt%, respectively, and traces of the following elements: As, Bi, Cd, Co, Cr, Cu, Fe, Ir, Mn, Mo, Ni, Os, Pb, Pd, Pt, Re, Ru, Se, Sb, Sn, Ta, Te, and V (Saager 1969; Feather and Koen 1975; Hallbauer and Utter 1977; Utter 1979; von Gehlen 1983; Hallbauer 1986; Oberthür and Saager 1986; Reid et al. 1988; Minter et al. 1990; Garayp et al. 1991; Frimmel et al. 1993; Frimmel and Gartz 1997). The presence of Cu in most of the gold analyses also sets the Jacobina gold apart, because in other metaconglomerate-hosted gold deposits Cu occurs only in trace amounts and has been attributed mostly to mineral inclusions (Frimmel et al. 1993; Frimmel and Gartz 1997). The EMPA elemental maps referred to above show Cu homogeneously distributed across the entire grains, suggesting that the metal is alloyed with gold (ESM Fig. 7). Also, analyses of externally remobilized gold feature as outliers in Cu-in-gold histograms with the highest Cu contents (ESM Fig. 6B), suggesting that gold may have been enriched in Cu during the most advanced stages of remobilization.

chunk_text: To assess the overall gold potential of the Roraima Supergroup, a comparison to the Witwatersrand goldfields in South Africa, the world's richest gold province with palaeoplacers (Frimmel and Nwaila 2020), seems pertinent. The overall sedimentology of the host rocks is strikingly similar as is the high number of erosional surfaces within the succession and its total thickness. A foreland basin setting has been envisaged for the particularly well-endowed Central Rand Basin in the Kaapvaal Craton. Similarly, such a setting seems plausible for the lower Roraima Supergroup, although it remains unclear whether it was in a retroarc position relative to the 1.94-1.93 Ga Rio Urubu magmatic arc. The 1901-1873 Ma upper Roraima Supergroup shows clear signs of proximity to arc magmatism at that time. A significant difference between the Roraima and Witwatersrand palaeoplacers is the gold source. For the former, this study revealed derivation from eroded discrete orogenic-type hydrothermal gold deposits in the hinterland, whereas the latter derived its gold primarily from the erosion of very fine-grained syn-depositional gold that had been fixed by microbes (Frimmel and Hennigh 2015 ). This difference in source, together with the much younger age established for the Roraima gold, predicts a much lower gold potential for the Roraima Supergroup if one follows the hypothesis of decreasing placer gold endowment over time from about 2.9 Ga onwards (Frimmel 2018). This notwithstanding, our new data attest to the Roraima Basin fill a certain potential for economic gold deposits. chunk_text: There is no doubt, based on the mode of occurrence and the morphology, that the gold particles in the Roraima Supergroup are detrital. Post-depositional introduction of gold by whatever hydrothermal or metamorphic fluids into the host conglomerates can be excluded because of the general lack of hydrothermal alteration and regional metamorphic overprint. No auriferous quartz veins have been noted anywhere in the study area. This raises the question as to the gold source. Simply based on the regional geological setting, basin architecture, palaeotransport directions and the variation in rounding of the detrital gold particles, a source in the nearby granitoid-greenstone terrane to the northeast seems likely. That area is well known for orogenic-type gold deposits, exemplified by the 2.0 Ga Omai deposit (Voicu et al. 1999). Erosion of similar deposits in the Palaeoproterozoic could well explain the Roraima detrital gold. Such an interpretation is corroborated by our Re-Os data. The low Os content of the gold particles is similar to that obtained for gold from hydrothermal deposits elsewhere and, thus, orders of magnitude lower than the Os content determined for gold particles from the richest reefs in the lower Central Rand Group in the Witwatersrand Basin (Frimmel et al. 2005). Although the Re-Os age obtained for the Roraima gold is subject to a huge error, it crudely overlaps with the age of orogenic-type hydrothermal gold mineralisation in the Transamazonian greenstone belt in the hinterland of the Roraima Basin.

title: Orogenic Gold Mineral Prospectivity Mapping (MPM) of the Geraldton Area, Ontario
chunk_text: Gold deposits in the Beardmore-Geraldton Belt are located within two main areas: the eastern Geraldton camp near the town of Geraldton and the western Beardmore camp immediately east of Lake Nipigon. The Bankfield-Tombill deformation zone hosts most of the deposits in the Geraldton camp including, from west to east, the Tombill, Bankfield, Consolidated Magnet, Consolidated Mosher Longlac, MacLeodCockshutt and Hard Rock deposits. The Hard Rock and McLeod-Cockshutt deposits were two of the three most prolific mines along the Bankfield-Tombill deformation. They produced 269,081 and 1,366,404 ounces of gold, respectively, from 1938 to 1966 (Mason and McConnell, 1983; Mason and White, 1986), and are being redeveloped as an open pit mine that will produce 5 million ounces of gold over the next 14 years (https://www.equinoxgold.com). The Bankfield-Tombill deformation zone is within the top northern section of the southern sedimentary unit, where intercalated gabbro, mafic volcanic rocks, feldspar-quartz porphyry, turbiditic sandstone, conglomerate and banded iron formation, are folded by tight isoclinal F 2 folds and transposed parallel to the strong east-southeast-striking foliation (S 2 ) that defines the Bankfield-Tombill deformation zone. Gold mineralization is present within all rock types and is preferentially associated with quartzcarbonate veins along sheared east-southeast-striking contacts between feldspar-quartz porphyry and sandstone, with quartz-carbonate veins and sulphide (pyrite, arsenopyrite) replacement lenses in banded iron formation, and with quartz-carbonate veins in massive sandstone and feldspar-quartz porphyry (Horwood and Pye, 1955; Pye, 1952; Anglin, 1987; Macdonald, 1988; Lavigne, 2009; Tóth, 2019). chunk_text: Petrographic examination reveals that the Menge area rocks have experienced low-grade metamorphism under greenschist facies conditions. The metadioritic rocks contain primary assemblages of plagioclase + hornblende + biotite ± quartz, with secondary chlorite, sericite and epidote reflecting hydrothermal alteration. Metavolcanic rocks display relict volcanic textures locally preserved despite metamorphic recrystallization. Primary assemblages include plagioclase + clinopyroxene ± olivine, with metamorphic overprints producing actinolite, chlorite and albite. Ore mineralogy is dominated by pyrite, pyrrhotite, chalcopyrite and sphalerite, with gold occurring as fine inclusions within sulfide phases or as free particles associated with quartz veining.

title: Lithological, Structural and Geochemical Characteristics of Gold Mineralization in the Menge Greenstone Belt, Western Ethiopia & Geochemical Signatures and Structural Controls of Gold Mineralization in the Menge District, Western Ethiopia
context_before: Geochemical signatures indicate evolved tholeiitic magmas of mantle origin with bimodal affinity. Hydrothermal alteration patterns include chloritization, sericitization, silicification and carbonatization.
chunk_text: The Menge area in the Benishangul-Gumuz Regional State of western Ethiopia represents a prospective gold mineralization zone within the Arabian-Nubian Shield. This study presents a comprehensive geochemical investigation of current gold deposits using field mapping, petrographic analysis and whole-rock geochemical data. Eight representative samples were analysed for major oxides and trace elements using XRF and ICP-MS techniques. The results reveal that gold mineralization is primarily hosted in shear zone-related quartz veins within low-grade metamorphic rocks including metadiorite, metagranite, metavolcanic rocks and quartzite. Gold concentrations range from 4.14 to 15.13 ppm, with the highest values associated with quartzite units. Assay values of up to 2.2 ppm Au and quartzite samples exceeding 15 ppm Au confirm significant gold enrichment. The mineralization style corresponds to mesothermal orogenic gold deposits, with hydrothermal fluids likely derived from metamorphic devolatilization. Geochemical signatures indicate evolved tholeiitic magmas of mantle origin with bimodal affinity. Hydrothermal alteration patterns include chloritization, sericitization, silicification and carbonatization. The structural setting, alteration assemblages and ore mineral paragenesis are consistent with mesothermal orogenic gold deposits similar to other Ethiopian gold occurrences. These findings suggest significant potential for economic gold mineralization in the western Ethiopian greenstone belt. Keywords: Gold deposits; Geochemistry; Arabian-nubian shield; Western Ethiopia; Orogenic gold; Hydrothermal alteration

chunk_text: The paper presents the results of a complex study of native gold from nine placers of the Murzinka group in the Middle Urals. Morphological features, chemical composition, and internal structure of native gold, as well as mineral inclusions within it, are described in detail. Based on the analysis of morphological characteristics and the gold particles rounding degree, the proximity of lode gold sources is inferred ranging from several hundred meters to the first few kilometers. Three types of native gold were identified according to the chemical composition and mineral inclusions. Type I (the predominant type) is characterized by high fineness with Ag and Hg admixture and inclusions of pyrite, chalcopyrite, galena, molybdenite, and petzite. The variation in admixture content within this type allows the definition of subtypes; their distribution in placers reflects the zoning of lode quartz gold mineralization. Type II is distinguished by elevated copper contents and bornite inclusions; Type III is defined by high Ag contents. Lode sources for the different gold types have been identified: for Type I, a quartz gold lode deposits; for Type II, precious metal mineralization in the gabbroids of the Pavdinsky massif. Application of the electron backscatter diffraction (EBSD) technique enabled a detailed characterization of the internal structure of gold particles. The observed high fineness intergranular veins and intergrowths of gold with minerals of the rhabdophane group suggest that native gold was located in the supergene zone during the period of active weathering crust development in the Upper Mesozoic and Palaeogene. It is established that the placer system in the Murzinka River basin formed during the Neogene-Quaternary period, primarily due to lode quartz gold mineralization. The obtained data allow the localization of prospective areas for the exploration of lode gold deposits and expand the understanding of the region's metallogenic potential.

chunk_text: The sedimentological makeup of the Roraima Supergroup with its numerous erosional unconformities, each overlain by quartz pebble conglomerate, is reminiscent of the Mesoarchaean Witwatersrand Supergroup in the Kaapvaal Craton of South Africa, which has become so famous for hosting the world's largest known regional concentration of gold (e.g. Frimmel and Nwaila 2020). The richest gold palaeoplacers formed during a gold mega-event at around 2.9 Ga, the prime representatives of which are the gold-rich quartz pebble conglomerates at the base of the Central Rand Group in the Witwatersrand Basin. Their formation has been attributed to the leaching of Au and subsequent transport as dissolved Au-sulfide complex from the Archaean land surface, followed by Au concentration due to an oxidative gradient induced by microbes, and the mechanical reworking of the gold-rich microbial mats to form conglomerate-hosted placers rich in micro-nuggets (Frimmel 2014; Mathur et al. 2025). Younger palaeoplacers derived the gold initially from older placers, but discrete endogenous gold deposits in the eroded hinterland became progressively important sources from c. 2.8 Ga onwards with an almost exponential decrease in total gold endowment and grade over time (Frimmel 2018). Although this notion leaves little room for giant, Witwatersrand-like gold placer deposits in post-Archaean sediment successions, a considerable potential remains for highly economic gold placers to exist in Palaeoproterozoic successions as exemplified by the > 2.4 Ga Jacobina depos - its in Brazil, the 2.45 Ga Pardo deposit in Canada, and the 2.10 Ga placers of Tarkwa, Ghana (Frimmel 2014). These circumstances provided strong motivation for gold exploration in the Roraima Supergroup.

chunk_text: A total of 51 boreholes were drilled, based on a 50 km 2 block system, at the localities Peaima, Mahaica, Eping and Chi Chi Falls all of which represent neighbouring areas along the northeastern escarpment of the Roraima Supergroup exposures as bounded by the Mazuruni River and its tributaries in the mining districts of Potaro and Mazaruni (Fig. 2, online supplementary material Table A1). A separate study area further southeast includes the locality of Parish's Hill (Fig. 2) at the head of the Demerara River where further 10 boreholes were drilled (online supplementary material Table A1). Several boreholes were defined as key stratigraphic holes and extended to investigate the underlying stratigraphy of the Roraima Supergroup below Unit IV as defined by Keats ( 1974). The boreholes were rotary drilled from surface to total depth using NQ core barrel providing cores of 46 mm in diameter. Core recovery was excellent, generally exceeding 99%. On completion of drilling, petrophysical measurements were conducted in each borehole, including gamma ray, density, porosity, magnetic susceptibility and resistivity measurements at a 100 mm sampling rate, and three-arm resistivity dipmeter measurements at a 10 mm sampling rate. Dipmeter resistivity curves were examined alongside the core description logs and important sedimentary surfaces were oriented to provide directional data for palaeotransport analysis. Based on sedimentological characteristics, selected intervals were sampled for further geochemical, petrological and geochronological analyses, as well as gold assays. chunk_text: The Jiaodong Peninsula is situated on the eastern margin of the North China Craton (NCC) and comprises two major tectonic units: the Jiaobei Terrane in the north and the Sulu Terrane in the south, bounded by the NNE-striking Wulian-Yantai Fault (Figure 1; Li et al., 2016). The Jiaobei Terrane is the primary host of gold mineralization in this region, with its basement predominantly dominated by Neoarchean Jiaodong Group, which chiefly consist of tonalite-trondhjemite-granodiorite (TTG) gneisses, granulites, and amphibolites. Mesozoic magmatism in the Jiaodong Peninsula, particularly the Early Cretaceous Guojialing, Weideshan, and Laoshan granites (130-113 Ma), is genetically associated with lithospheric thinning of the North China Craton (Goldfarb and Santosh, 2014; Yang et al., 2016a) and intense crust-mantle interaction (Goss et al., 2010; Guo et al., 2013; Tang et al., 2014), providing critical thermal energy, fluids, and material contributions for gold mineralization. Specifically, the thermal and dynamic effects of magmatic intrusions can regulate fluid migration and gold precipitation, especially in gently dipping fault segments where stable pressure conditions facilitate prolonged fluid-rock interaction and mineral deposition (Song et al., 2012; Song et al., 2015).

title: Integrating machine learning with numerical simulation for 3D mineral prospectivity modeling in the Sanshandao-Haiyu gold belt, Eastern China
chunk_text: In summary, the Sanshandao fault is characterized by a steepto-gentle dip transition, which governs the migration pathways of gold-bearing hydrothermal fluids and wall-rock metasomatism, consequently leading to a stepwise spatial distribution of mineralization (Yang et al., 2006; Song et al., 2012; Song et al., 2015). Numerical modeling indicates that positive volumetric strain is preferentially localized within gently dipping fault segments, generating structurally controlled, dilatant ore-hosting zones (Figure 7A). During the upward migration of large-scale orebearing hydrothermal fluids from depth to shallow crust, the gently dipping fault segments, with a relatively flat geometry and lateral confinement by steeply dipping fault segments at their two ends, induce a reduced fluid migration rate and thus prolong the temporal window for mineralization (Boullier and Robert, 1992; Cox, 1995; Robert et al., 1995). As processes such as pressure release, temperature reduction, and fluid mixing occur, the stability of gold-bearing complexes is disrupted, thereby promoting the development of gold-bearing hydrothermal mineralization processes (Williams-Jones et al., 2009; Figure 7B). FIGURE 7 (A) Volumetric strain and (B) gold precipitation distributions. Note that negative rate values indicate gold mineralization formation.
